explainers.title: Hello and welcome to Reflection
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. You have already grown three thinking skills this year. Now you reach one of the most powerful of all, because it is about you: Reflection.

Remember, there are six thinking skills in Global Perspectives, and you grow all of them, year by year:

The first three skills point outwards, at the world. Reflection is different: it points inwards, at yourself and at your team. It means stopping after you have done something, looking back honestly, and asking: what did I learn, how have my ideas changed, what did I do well in my group, and what could I do better next time?

This matters far beyond school. Think of a footballer who watches a video of the last match to see what to fix, a nurse who thinks about how to comfort the next worried patient, or a shopkeeper who works out why one week sold better than another. All of them are reflecting. People who look back and learn from their own experience get better, faster, at almost everything. That is the skill you will start to build here.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong an idea or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn, how you work in a team, and how you have changed.
Collaboration — working well together with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so that others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in the Ehel Academy way, which means three kinds of support work together. Reflection needs a special version of this, because reflection is really about teamwork, and teamwork needs real people.

So this unit has a clear rhythm. You do the real teamwork with your group in your teacher sessions, and with your family and community at home. Then you reflect on it with your AI tutor, on your own time, and turn what you noticed into a strong written reflection.

Think of it like sport again. Your teacher session is the real match, where you play alongside your team. Your time with your AI tutor is the quiet moment afterwards, when a good player thinks back over the game and works out how to play even better next time. In the old style of this subject, learners were told to 'discuss with a partner' or 'give feedback to your group'. In our model, you do that thinking with your AI tutor, and you carry your best ideas back to your real team.
bullets: You, at your own pace. Reflection is naturally a quiet, personal skill. You write your own reflections in your own time, thinking honestly about your own work. Nobody can do that part for you.

Your AI tutor, ready any time, day or night. Your tutor is your reflection partner. Before a team project it helps you plan your contribution. Afterwards it helps you talk through what went well and what was hard, and it helps you draft your written reflection until it is clear, honest and complete.
Your teacher and your team, about twice a week. This is where the real teamwork happens. You work face to face with your group on a shared project, take a team role, and see how a real team feels.

explainers.title: Meet Aran and his team
explainers.body:
To make each part of reflection clear, we will follow one Year 6 learner all through the unit. His name is Aran, and he is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

Aran is not on his own. He works in a small team with three classmates: Leila, Sami and Nadia. Over the year, this team takes on several shared Challenges, and Aran keeps a journal of what he learns each time. We will watch him reflect on three real team projects:

You will also see Aran's team disagree, run out of time, and get a few things wrong. That is completely normal. Every real team struggles sometimes. What makes Aran's team a good team is not that they never have problems. It is that they keep working together kindly, and afterwards they look back honestly and learn. Your own team will be just the same, and that is nothing to worry about.
bullets: Reducing plastic waste at school — the team notices how many plastic bags and water sachets are thrown away each day, and plans a 'plastic-free week'.
Protecting bees and local crops — the team finds out how bees pollinate crops and wild plants near Hargeisa, and makes a poster to help protect them.
A healthy-eating campaign — the team plans a short assembly and poster to help younger children choose healthier snacks and drinks.

explainers.title: Your Challenge and your reflection journal
explainers.body:
In this unit you will not only read about Aran. You will do your own team Challenge, agreed with your group in a teacher session, and you will reflect on it just as he does. Your Challenge could be any shared project that matters where you live, such as cutting litter in the schoolyard, saving water, welcoming new pupils, or making break times fairer.

To help you, start one simple habit that all good learners use: keep a reflection journal. This can be a notebook or a document where you write down what you learn about yourself and your team, a little at a time. It becomes the store of everything you notice, and it makes writing your final reflection far easier.

explainers.title: What is reflection, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think reflection just means saying 'that was fun' or 'that was hard' and moving on. Real reflection is deeper than that. Reflection means thinking about an experience in depth: what you learned, how your ideas and behaviour changed, how your skills are growing, what you did for your team, and the good parts and the hard parts of working together.

Good reflection is always honest and balanced. Honest means you tell the truth about your own part, even the tricky bits. Balanced means you talk about what went well and what was hard, not just one or the other. A reflection that only praises you, or only complains, is not yet a strong reflection.

explainers.title: Reflecting on what you learned and how your ideas changed
explainers.body: One of the best things about a project is that it can change your mind. At the start you think one thing, and by the end, after you have found things out, you think something new. A strong reflection notices this change and says it clearly. A useful sentence frame is: I used to think ... but now I think ...

explainers.title: Reflecting on a skill you got better at
explainers.body: Every project helps you get better at something. It might be a big skill like speaking to a group, or a smaller one like keeping tidy notes or drawing a clear picture. A strong reflection names one skill and says how you improved it and why you needed to. A useful frame is: Before I could not ... now I have got better at ... because I needed to ...

explainers.title: Your contribution to the team
explainers.body:
In a team, everyone should do something that helps. The thing you do is called your contribution. A strong reflection says clearly what you personally did, without either boasting or hiding. A useful frame is: One thing I personally did to help the team was ...

Your contribution does not have to be the biggest or the loudest job. Quiet, steady help is just as valuable. Here are contributions that all really matter in a team:
bullets: Keeping clear notes so the team remembers its decisions.
Making sure a quieter member gets a turn to speak.
Checking the time so the team finishes its work.
Finding a useful fact, or drawing a clear picture.
Calming a disagreement so the team can carry on.

explainers.title: The benefits and challenges of teamwork
explainers.body: Working in a team has clear benefits, but it also brings real challenges. A balanced reflection is honest about both. If you only ever say teamwork is wonderful, or only ever say it is annoying, you are not reflecting fully.
bullets: Benefits: more ideas than one person could have, the work shared out so it is lighter, and different people who are good at different things.
Challenges: people disagree, someone may not do their share, it can be hard to make a decision, and it takes time to organise everyone.

explainers.title: Team roles: who does what
explainers.body:
Teams work better when everyone has a clear role. A role is a special job that helps the whole group. In Global Perspectives there are four roles that make teamwork run smoothly:

It is fair to swap roles between projects, so that everyone gets a turn at each. When you reflect, it helps to name your role, because your role shapes what you contributed and which skills you used.
bullets: Facilitator — makes sure everyone takes part and that the team stays friendly and on topic.
Recorder — keeps clear notes of what the team decides.
Reporter — tells the class or the assembly what the team found or made.
Timekeeper — watches the clock so the team finishes its work in the time it has.

explainers.title: Planning and fairly dividing the team's tasks
explainers.body:
A big project is really a set of smaller tasks. A good team lists the tasks, then shares them out fairly, so that no one person does everything and no one is left with nothing. A simple task plan answers four questions for each task: What needs doing? Who will do it? How will they do it? When, and how long will it take?

Clever teams also let some tasks happen at the same time, which we call working in parallel. While one person does one task, another person does a different one, so the whole project finishes faster.

explainers.title: Writing a complete and balanced personal reflection
explainers.body:
Now you can put the parts together into a full personal reflection. A complete, balanced reflection covers all of these, in your own words:

That last point is the key to balance: a strong reflection always includes both the good and the hard. Leaving out the hard parts makes it sound boastful; leaving out the good parts makes it sound gloomy. Real reflection tells the whole story.
bullets: The issue you worked on, and why it matters.
Your team's goal, and the action you took.
Your own contribution, told honestly.
How you could improve your contribution next time.
What was good about working as a team, and what was hard.

explainers.title: How new information and other people change your thinking
explainers.body: The deepest kind of reflection notices how you have changed because of a project. New facts and other people's ideas can change three things: what you think about the issue, how you behave, and the skills you have. A strong reflection can even explain the link between what you learned and what you then decided to do.
bullets: Your thoughts: Before, I used to think ... now I realise ... because ...
Your behaviour: Before I used to ... now I ... because I now know that ...
Your skills: Before I could not ... now I can ... because I needed to ...

explainers.title: Matching teamwork challenges to solutions
explainers.body: Every team meets challenges. The clever move is to notice the challenge and then find a sensible solution, so the same problem does not spoil your next project. Reflecting on a challenge is only really finished when you can say what you would do differently.

explainers.title: Giving constructive feedback
explainers.body: Sometimes you reflect on your own work, and sometimes you help someone else reflect on theirs by giving feedback. Good feedback is constructive, which means it is kind and helpful, and it always includes something that was done well and a clear idea for improving. Two friendly frames are: Well done for ... and Next time you could try ...

explainers.title: How Reflection makes your other skills stronger
explainers.body:
Reflection is special because it feeds back into every other skill. Each time you look back honestly, your next attempt at everything gets better.

So the honest thinking you do in this unit is never wasted. It is the skill that quietly lifts all the others.
bullets: Research improves when you reflect on which sources helped you and which wasted your time.
Analysis improves when you notice which of your reasons turned out to be strong.
Evaluation improves as you get better at judging your own work, not just other people's.
Collaboration improves the most, because reflecting on your teamwork shows you exactly how to be a better teammate.
Communication improves when you reflect on whether your audience really understood you.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: Aran's whole journey
explainers.body: You have now met every part of reflection. Here is how they came together across Aran's year, from a busy team project to a thoughtful, honest reflection.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Collaboration. Reflection and Collaboration are close friends: reflection shows you how to work with others better, and collaboration gives you the real teamwork to reflect on. Everything you have practised here about roles, contributions, benefits and challenges will make you a much stronger member of any team. Well done for looking honestly at your own learning; that is one of the bravest and most useful things a learner can do.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: Reflection is like looking in a mirror after a busy day, but you look at what you did and what you learned, not at your face.
You cannot change the past, but you can learn from it. Every reflection makes your next attempt a little bit better.
In this unit the team projects are the vehicle. The real prize is becoming a person who learns from everything they do.

bigIdeas.title: What to write in your reflection journal
lines: The date, and which team project you worked on that day.
Your role in the team, and one thing you did to help.
One thing that went well, and one thing that was hard.
One way your ideas or your skills changed, however small.
One thing you want to do better next time.

bigIdeas.title: Being fair to different families
lines: In a healthy-eating project, remember that families eat differently for many reasons, including custom and belief.
At some times of year many families change how they eat: for example, many Muslim families fast during Ramadan, and some Christian families fast during Lent.
A fair campaign respects all of these, and shares helpful ideas without telling anyone their family is wrong. Listening to other perspectives is part of reflecting well.

bigIdeas.title: A model: what a complete reflection looks like
lines: The issue we worked on was protecting bees, which is important because bees pollinate the crops that feed us.
Our goal was to make a poster for the school. The action we took was to design and print it together.
My contribution was finding the main image and keeping our notes. I could have improved by checking on my teammates halfway.
Working as a team helped us because we shared the tasks. It was challenging because we disagreed about the slogan, but we solved it by voting.
I used to think bees only make honey, but now I know they pollinate our food crops too.

bigIdeas.title: Your team Challenge runs through everything
lines: With your group, agree one shared project that matters where you live, such as cutting litter, saving water, or welcoming new pupils.
You will reflect on this same Challenge in every activity, so choose something you all care about.
By the end you will have a complete, honest reflection you can be proud of.

bigIdeas.title: A reflection to check
lines: Our team worked on saving water at school. Our goal was to stop taps being left running. I designed the reminder signs for the taps. It went really well and everyone liked my signs. I think I did a great job.
Now check it against these questions. For each one, write 'yes' or 'no':

bigIdeas.title: A weak reflection to respond to
lines: Aran's teammate wrote: I helped with the bee poster. It was good. I do not really know what else to say.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 4 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Reflection.
Ask it: In one or two simple sentences, why is it useful to look back and reflect after working in a team?
Then tell your tutor about a time you worked with others, at school or at home, and say one thing that went well and one thing that was hard.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think reflection means.
Ask it: Is my idea of reflection missing anything important?
Then ask the tutor to give you one everyday example of reflection that has nothing to do with school.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor one thing you have found out in a project this year.
Ask it to help you finish the sentence: I used to think ... but now I think ...
Then ask the tutor: What is it about the new information that changed my mind?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a skill you think you got a little better at this year.
Ask it to help you finish: Before I could not ... now I have got better at ... because ...
Ask the tutor to suggest one small way you could keep improving that same skill.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a team activity you did, at school or at home.
Ask it to help you finish: One thing I personally did to help the team was ...
Then ask the tutor: Was there anything else I did to help that I have not noticed?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a team you have worked in.
Ask it to help you name one clear benefit and one clear challenge of working in that team.
Then ask the tutor: What is one thing the team could do to make that challenge smaller next time?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Ask your AI tutor to explain the four team roles back to you in its own words.
Tell it which role you think would suit you best right now, and which would stretch you the most.
Then plan with the tutor how you would do that stretching role well, ready to try it with your team.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a project your team needs to do.
Ask it to help you list the tasks and suggest which ones could be done in parallel, at the same time.
Then take your draft plan to your team in your teacher session and agree the real who-does-what together.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a real team project you have done.
Ask it to help you write a few sentences covering the issue, your goal and action, your contribution, how to improve, and what was good and hard.
Then ask the tutor: Is my reflection complete and balanced, or is a part missing?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about something you learned that changed how you act, not just how you think.
Ask it to help you explain the link: what did you learn, and what did you then decide to do differently?
Then ask the tutor whether another person's idea has ever changed your mind, and how.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about a challenge your team met.
Ask it to help you think of one practical solution you could try next time.
Then ask the tutor for one more challenge that teams often meet, and work out a solution for that one too.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read a reflection you have written to your AI tutor, and ask it to give you constructive feedback: one thing done well, one thing to improve.
Then practise the other way round: ask the tutor for a short example reflection, and you give it constructive feedback using Well done for and Next time you could try.
Ask the tutor whether your feedback was kind, specific and helpful.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your team Challenge and your two feelings from step 3.
Ask it: What is one thing I could do to make the part I feel unsure about go better?
Ask the tutor to remind you what makes a reflection journal useful.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which role you would like and which would stretch you.
Ask it to help you plan how to do a stretching role well, so you feel ready to try it.
Ask the tutor why it is fair for a team to swap roles between projects.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your task grid to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Are any tasks shared unfairly, and which ones could we do in parallel to save time?
Ask the tutor to suggest a sensible order for the tasks.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your 'I used to think ... but now I think ...' sentence to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your changed idea is clear, and what made it change.
Ask the tutor to help you notice one more way your thinking has grown this year.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your benefit, your challenge and your solution to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your reflection is balanced, with both a good part and a hard part.
Ask the tutor for one more benefit of teamwork that you may not have noticed.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain, simply, any that you found tricky.
Then ask the tutor: which of these six skills do I most want to get better at, and why?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which parts of the reflection were missing.
Read your improved version and ask: Is it now complete and balanced?
Ask the tutor to point to any part that is still missing or unclear.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five pairs to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it which challenge your own team is most likely to meet, and why.
Ask the tutor to help you plan ahead so that challenge is smaller next time.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your feedback to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your feedback is kind, specific and helpful.
Ask the tutor to show you one other polite way to suggest an improvement.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your full reflection to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Is my reflection complete, honest and balanced? Which part is strongest, and which is weakest?
Ask the tutor to help you improve the weakest part until you are proud of the whole reflection.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three checkpoint sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you turn your 'one thing I will do differently' into a clear, small goal.
Ask the tutor to remind you of this goal at the start of your next team project.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three improved reflections to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether each one is now honest, balanced and complete.
Ask the tutor to show you one more way to improve the reflection you found hardest.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your five answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to tell you which answer was strongest and why.
Ask the tutor to give you one more situation like these to try.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your reflection answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to help you notice how your thinking changed from the start of the unit to now.
Ask the tutor to suggest one part of reflection to keep working on during the Collaboration unit, and why.

speakingPrompts.title: A human touch
lines: Ask someone at home to tell you about a time they worked in a team, at work or in the community.
Ask them: what was good about working together, and what was hard?
Write their answer in your reflection journal, and bring it to your next teacher session.

speakingPrompts.title: Share it at home
lines: Read your finished reflection to someone at home.
Ask them what they think you have learned this year, and add anything new to your journal.

teacherSessions.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Share your Challenge with your group and agree it together in your next teacher session.
Agree how often you will each add to your own reflection journals.

teacherSessions.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Agree who will take each role for your Challenge, making sure the choice is fair.
Plan to swap roles next time so everyone gets a turn at each.

teacherSessions.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Agree the real task grid together, and write down who has promised to do what.
Halfway through the project, check in with each other to see how the tasks are going.

teacherSessions.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Share your benefits and challenges with your group and see how many you agree on.
Together, choose one challenge to work on so your next project runs more smoothly.

teacherSessions.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Swap short reflections with a partner in your group and give each other constructive feedback out loud.
Thank each other for the feedback, and use it to improve your own reflection.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran looks back on the plastic-free week
lines: A weak reflection would just say: The plastic-free week was good. I liked it.

Aran's stronger reflection says: Our goal was to cut the plastic our class throws away. I kept the notes so we remembered our decisions. It went well because everyone brought a cloth bag. It was hard because two people forgot on the first day, so next time we would put up a reminder poster.
Notice how the stronger reflection has a goal, his own contribution, something good, and something hard. That is reflection in depth.

Through the rest of this file, you will meet each part of reflection, one at a time, with an example from Aran's team and a step you can do with your AI tutor. Keep your reflection journal open as you read.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's example: his ideas about bees changed
lines: Before the bee project, Aran used to think bees were just insects that sting and make honey.

Now he thinks very differently. He says: I used to think bees only make honey, but now I know they pollinate crops and wild plants here in the Horn of Africa, so without bees our food would be scarcer and more expensive.
That is a real change of ideas, caused by what he learned. He even changed what he does: he now helps his family grow flowering plants that bees like.

Changed ideas are worth celebrating, not hiding. Changing your mind because of good evidence is a sign of a strong thinker, not a weak one. In your reflection, try to name one clear thing you believe now that you did not believe before, and say what taught you the new idea.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's example: getting better at speaking to a group
lines: For the healthy-eating assembly, Aran had to say part of the talk out loud in front of younger children.

He reflects: Before, I could not look up while I was speaking, because I felt nervous. Now I have got better at it, because my team let me practise with them three times, so by the assembly I could look at the children and speak slowly.
Aran names the skill (speaking), says how it improved (practice with his team), and why he needed to (the assembly). That is a complete skill reflection.

You do not have to be brilliant at the skill yet. 'Getting better' is enough. Even a small step forward, clearly noticed, shows that you are learning. Keep a list in your reflection journal of skills you are improving, and add to it after every project.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's example: his contribution to the plastic project
lines: In the plastic-free week, Aran was the team's recorder, so his job was to write down what the group decided.

He reflects: One thing I personally did to help was keep clear notes. When Sami forgot what we had agreed about the reminder poster, I could read it back from my notes, so the team did not waste time arguing.
That is a modest but real contribution, described honestly.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's example: a benefit and a challenge
lines: Aran reflects on the plastic project like this.
A benefit: Working as a team helped us because Nadia thought of using cloth bags, which I would never have thought of on my own.
A challenge: Working as a team was hard because one member missed a deadline, so our poster was rushed. Next time we would check on each other halfway through.
By naming one of each, Aran gives a fair, balanced picture of teamwork.

Every team meets challenges like these. A team in Mogadishu working on a street clean-up would face them too, and so will yours. Noticing a challenge is not complaining. It is the first step to fixing it. Later in this unit you will learn how to match common teamwork challenges to sensible solutions, so that your next project runs more smoothly.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's example: his team shares out the roles
lines: For the bee project, Aran's team agreed roles at the start: Leila was the facilitator, Aran was the recorder, Nadia was the reporter, and Sami was the timekeeper.
Aran reflects: Being the recorder helped me get better at writing quick, tidy notes. Next project I would like to try being the reporter, so I can practise speaking to the class.
Naming his role helped Aran see both what he did and what he wants to try next.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's example: planning the bee poster
lines: The team's tasks were: find a strong image of a bee, write a short slogan, gather three key facts, design the layout, and print copies.
They shared them out: Aran found the image because he is good at drawing, while at the same time Nadia wrote the slogan and Sami gathered the facts. That is working in parallel.
Aran reflects: Sharing the tasks was fair, and doing them at the same time meant we finished in one lesson instead of two.

When you reflect on a project, it is worth asking whether the tasks were shared fairly. If one person did far too much, or too little, that is something the team can put right next time by planning more carefully at the start.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's example: a complete reflection on the bee project
lines: The issue we worked on was protecting bees, which matters because bees pollinate the crops that feed us.
Our goal was to make a poster to teach the school why bees are important. The action we took was to design and print the poster together.
My contribution was finding the main image and keeping our notes. I could have improved by checking on my teammates halfway, because our first plan slipped.
Working as a team helped us because we shared the tasks. It was hard because we disagreed about the slogan, but we solved it by voting.

Notice that Aran's reflection is honest and balanced, and it touches every part. You will practise writing your own full reflection in the Activities file, with your AI tutor helping you check that nothing important is missing.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's example: the healthy-eating project changed him
lines: New facts changed his thoughts: Before, Aran used to think fruit juice was always healthy; now he realises many juices have lots of sugar, because he read it while researching.
That changed his behaviour: Before he drank juice every day; now he often chooses water, because he knows why it is better.
Another person changed his mind too: Nadia suggested asking families what snacks they already liked, and Aran realised their campaign would work better if it respected what people were used to.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's example: turning challenges into solutions
lines: Challenge: We were not sure if our plastic-free week had actually worked. Solution: next time, decide how to measure success before we start, such as counting the bags of rubbish before and after.
Challenge: Some families did not want to change their snack habits. Solution: show real examples from another school where the change helped, so people can see it is possible.
Challenge: Everyone had different ideas and some jobs were left undone. Solution: make a clear task plan that says who does what and by when.

You will find a fuller challenges-and-solutions table in your Skills Toolkit. The habit to build is simple: whenever you name a problem in your reflection, follow it straight away with an idea for solving it.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's example: helping a teammate reflect
lines: Sami wrote a short reflection that only said: I did my part and it was fine.
Aran gives constructive feedback: Well done for finishing your facts on time, that really helped us. Next time you could try saying one thing that was hard, so your reflection shows the whole story.
Aran is kind and specific. He praises a real action and suggests one clear improvement, so Sami feels helped, not criticised.

Constructive feedback is never about being nice and saying nothing, and it is never about being harsh. It sits in the middle: honest, specific and kind. When you give it well, your whole team gets better together.

reflectionPrompts.title: Aran's journey, from doing to reflecting
lines: He worked in a team on three Challenges: plastic waste, protecting bees, and healthy eating.
He took different roles, made a fair task plan, and worked in parallel with his teammates.
He noticed how his ideas changed, and which skills, like speaking, he got better at.
He wrote complete, balanced reflections that named his contribution and both the good and the hard.
He turned challenges into solutions, and he learned to give a teammate kind, constructive feedback.

By reflecting like this, Aran did not just finish some projects. He became a stronger learner and a better teammate, ready for whatever comes next. In the Activities file, you will do the very same thing with your own team Challenge, one step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you.

reflectionPrompts.title: A model: how one team shared the roles
lines: Karim's team agreed roles at the start of their litter project. Yasmin was the facilitator, so she made sure quiet Layla got a turn. Omar was the timekeeper and gave a warning at five minutes left.
Karim was the recorder and Idris was the reporter. Because each person had a clear job, nobody was left out and nothing important was forgotten.

reflectionPrompts.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: I used to think littering was just a bit untidy, but now I think it is a real danger, because I learned that plastic blocks drains and can be washed to the coast near Berbera, where it harms sea animals.
What taught me the new idea: a fact I found while researching, and seeing a blocked drain near school.

reflectionPrompts.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: A benefit: Working as a team helped us because Nadia thought of an idea I would never have had on my own.
A challenge: It was hard because we disagreed about the design, which wasted time. Next time we would vote quickly instead of arguing.

toolkit.title: The Reflection skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Reflection means thinking about an experience in depth: what you learned, how your ideas and behaviour changed, how your skills are growing, what you did for your team, and the good parts and the hard parts of working together. It is not just saying 'that was fun' and moving on.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always be honest about your own part, including the tricky bits. Second, always be balanced, talking about what was good and what was hard. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

Why bother? Because reflection is how you get better on purpose. Anyone can finish a project and move on. A learner who stops to think 'what worked, what did not, and what will I change next time' improves far faster. Every honest reflection makes your next team, your next project and your next attempt a little stronger.

toolkit.title: Your Stage 6 Reflection learning goals
toolkit.intro: Your reflection skills grow in three stages this year. Here are the real learning goals for each stage, in simple words. Your teacher may talk about these.

toolkit.title: The four team roles
toolkit.intro: Teams work best when everyone has a clear role. Swap roles between projects so everyone gets a turn at each.

rows: Facilitator
Makes sure everyone takes part and the team stays friendly and on topic.
Amal has not spoken yet; let us hear her idea.
Recorder
Keeps clear notes of what the team decides.
So we agreed to make a poster, not a video. I have written that down.
Reporter
Tells the class or the assembly what the team found or made.
Our team found that we throw away many plastic bags each day.
Timekeeper
Watches the clock so the team finishes in the time it has.
We have ten minutes left, so let us choose our final idea.

toolkit.title: Template: planning and sharing the tasks
toolkit.intro:
Break your project into small tasks, then share them out fairly. Let some tasks happen at the same time (in parallel) to finish faster. Copy this grid and fill in one row per task.

Then check two things: is the share fair, and could any tasks be done in parallel to save time?

rows: Find a strong image
Write a short slogan
Gather the key facts
Design the layout

toolkit.title: Frame: a complete and balanced personal reflection
toolkit.intro:
A strong reflection covers every part below. Finish each sentence starter in your own words, and always include both the good and the hard.

To show how you have changed, add one or two of these:
items: The issue we worked on was ...
This issue is important because ...
Our goal was ...
The action we took was ...
My contribution was ...
I could have improved my contribution by ...
Working as a team helped us to ...
Working as a team was challenging because ...
I used to think ... but now I think ...
Before I could not ... now I have got better at ... because ...
Before I used to ... now I ... because I now know that ...

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for benefits and challenges
toolkit.intro: Use these to talk in a balanced way about teamwork. Always give at least one of each.
items: A benefit was that working as a team let us ...
Another good thing about our teamwork was ...
A challenge we met was ...
This was hard because ...
Next time we could make it easier by ...

toolkit.title: Table: teamwork challenges and solutions
toolkit.intro: When you name a challenge in your reflection, follow it with a solution. This table gives common ones.

rows: We were not sure if our plan had worked.
Decide how to measure success before we start.
We spent time on a problem that was not really there.
Do a short survey first to find the real need.
People had different ideas and some jobs were undone.
Make a clear task plan saying who does what and by when.
We could not present because it was test week.
Make a timetable that takes other school events into account.
Others did not know what our team was doing.
Put up a display board with our plan, dates and goal.
People did not want to change an old habit.
Show real examples from another school where the change helped.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for constructive feedback
toolkit.intro:
Good feedback is kind and helpful. Name a strength and an improvement. Use these starters:

Avoid feedback that is empty ('It was fine') or harsh ('That was bad'). Aim for the honest, kind middle.
items: Well done for ...
One thing you did really well was ...
Next time you could try ...
It might be even stronger if ...
Have you thought about ...?

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for showing you have changed
toolkit.intro: Use these to show how a project changed your thoughts, your behaviour, or your skills:
items: Before, I used to think ... now I realise ... because ...
Before I used to ... however, now I ... because I now know that ...
Before I could not ... now I can ... because I needed to ...
Another person's idea changed my mind when ...

toolkit.title: Quick checklist: is my reflection strong?
toolkit.intro: Before you finish a reflection, read it back and tick each line. If you cannot tick them all, add the missing part.
items: It names the issue and why it matters.
It gives the goal and the action the team took.
It describes my own contribution honestly, without boasting or hiding.
It says how I could improve my contribution next time.
It includes something that was good AND something that was hard.
It shows one clear way my ideas or my skills have changed.

challenge.intro: A balanced reflection is honest about the good parts and the hard parts of teamwork. This activity helps you capture both, so your final reflection tells the whole story.
topics: Think about your team Challenge so far. Write one clear benefit: something that was better because you worked as a team, not alone.
Now write one clear challenge: something that was harder because you worked as a team.
For your challenge, write one idea for making it smaller next time.
Finish this sentence honestly: 'On the whole, working as a team was worth it because ...'.
checkpoints: The most important thing I learned about myself is ...
The most important thing I learned about teamwork is ...
The one thing I will do differently in my next team is ...

activities.title: Start your reflection journal
activities.label: Activity 1: Start your reflection journal
activities.intro: A reflection journal is where you store what you learn about yourself and your team. Start yours now, and you will thank yourself later, because your final reflection will almost write itself.
steps: Write today's date and the name of your team Challenge at the top of a new page.
Write one sentence: 'The reason our team chose this Challenge is ...'.
Write one thing you are looking forward to about working in this team, and one thing you feel unsure about.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor your team Challenge and your two feelings from step 3.
Ask it: What is one thing I could do to make the part I feel unsure about go better?
Ask the tutor to remind you what makes a reflection journal useful.

boxes.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Share your Challenge with your group and agree it together in your next teacher session.
Agree how often you will each add to your own reflection journals.

activities.title: Assign your team roles
activities.label: Activity 2: Assign your team roles
activities.intro: Teams run smoothly when everyone has a clear role. Remember the four roles: facilitator (makes sure everyone takes part), recorder (keeps notes), reporter (tells the class), and timekeeper (watches the clock).
steps: Write the four roles in your journal, with one sentence saying what each one does.
Decide which role would suit you best right now, and which would stretch you the most.
Write one thing you would do to carry out your chosen role well.

boxes.title: A model: how one team shared the roles
lines: Karim's team agreed roles at the start of their litter project. Yasmin was the facilitator, so she made sure quiet Layla got a turn. Omar was the timekeeper and gave a warning at five minutes left.
Karim was the recorder and Idris was the reporter. Because each person had a clear job, nobody was left out and nothing important was forgotten.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which role you would like and which would stretch you.
Ask it to help you plan how to do a stretching role well, so you feel ready to try it.
Ask the tutor why it is fair for a team to swap roles between projects.

boxes.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Agree who will take each role for your Challenge, making sure the choice is fair.
Plan to swap roles next time so everyone gets a turn at each.

activities.title: Plan and fairly divide the tasks
activities.label: Activity 3: Plan and fairly divide the tasks
activities.intro:
A big project is a set of smaller tasks. Plan them with a simple grid that answers four questions: What needs doing, Who will do it, How they will do it, and When, and how long it will take. Try to let some tasks happen at the same time, which is called working in parallel.

Copy this grid into your journal and fill in one row for each task your Challenge needs.

When your grid is full, check it is fair: has anyone been given far too much, or too little? Change the grid until the share feels even.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your task grid to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Are any tasks shared unfairly, and which ones could we do in parallel to save time?
Ask the tutor to suggest a sensible order for the tasks.

boxes.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Agree the real task grid together, and write down who has promised to do what.
Halfway through the project, check in with each other to see how the tasks are going.

activities.title: 'I used to think ... now I think ...'
activities.label: Activity 4: 'I used to think ... now I think ...'
activities.intro: One of the clearest signs of learning is a changed mind. This activity captures how your ideas have grown during your Challenge.
steps: Think back to the very start of your Challenge. Write one thing you believed about the topic then.
Now write what you believe about it today, after finding things out.
Join them with the frame: 'I used to think ... but now I think ...'.
Write one sentence saying what taught you the new idea (a fact, an experience, or another person).

boxes.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: I used to think littering was just a bit untidy, but now I think it is a real danger, because I learned that plastic blocks drains and can be washed to the coast near Berbera, where it harms sea animals.
What taught me the new idea: a fact I found while researching, and seeing a blocked drain near school.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your 'I used to think ... but now I think ...' sentence to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your changed idea is clear, and what made it change.
Ask the tutor to help you notice one more way your thinking has grown this year.

activities.title: Which skill does the reflection show?
activities.label: Activity 5: Which skill does the reflection show?
activities.intro: A reflection can show any of the six Global Perspectives skills. Read each statement below and decide which skill it shows: Research, Analysis, Evaluation, Reflection, Collaboration, or Communication. Write the pairs, such as 1-Analysis.
steps: 'I checked whether the website that said bees do not matter could be trusted, and found it had no author.'
'I worked out that one big cause of our litter was single-use water sachets.'
'The question our team investigated was: does our school use too much plastic?'
'I made sure everyone in the group had a turn to speak.'
'I looked back and noticed that my idea about bees had completely changed.'
'I explained our findings to the assembly in a clear, simple way.'

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain, simply, any that you found tricky.
Then ask the tutor: which of these six skills do I most want to get better at, and why?

activities.title: Is this reflection complete and balanced?
activities.label: Activity 6: Is this reflection complete and balanced?
activities.intro:
A complete, balanced reflection covers the issue, the goal and action, the writer's contribution, how they could improve, and what was good and hard. Read the short reflection below and use the checklist to judge it.

Then rewrite the reflection so that every answer becomes 'yes'. Add the missing parts in your own words.
steps: Does it name the issue and why it matters?
Does it give the goal and the action?
Does it describe the writer's own contribution?
Does it say how the writer could improve next time?
Does it include something that was hard, not only what was good?

boxes.title: A reflection to check
lines: Our team worked on saving water at school. Our goal was to stop taps being left running. I designed the reminder signs for the taps. It went really well and everyone liked my signs. I think I did a great job.
Now check it against these questions. For each one, write 'yes' or 'no':

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor which parts of the reflection were missing.
Read your improved version and ask: Is it now complete and balanced?
Ask the tutor to point to any part that is still missing or unclear.

activities.title: Write constructive feedback
activities.label: Activity 7: Write constructive feedback
activities.intro: Constructive feedback is kind and helpful. It names one thing done well and one clear idea for improving, using frames like Well done for ... and Next time you could try ...
steps: Write one thing this reflection does that is worth praising, starting with 'Well done for ...'.
Write one clear way it could be improved, starting with 'Next time you could try ...'.
Check your feedback is kind, specific and helpful, not harsh and not empty.

boxes.title: A weak reflection to respond to
lines: Aran's teammate wrote: I helped with the bee poster. It was good. I do not really know what else to say.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your feedback to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your feedback is kind, specific and helpful.
Ask the tutor to show you one other polite way to suggest an improvement.

boxes.title: With your team (teacher session)
lines: Swap short reflections with a partner in your group and give each other constructive feedback out loud.
Thank each other for the feedback, and use it to improve your own reflection.

activities.title: Write your own complete reflection
activities.label: Activity 8: Write your own complete reflection
activities.intro:
This is the big one. Using everything you have practised, write a full, honest, balanced reflection on your team Challenge. The sentence starters below cover every part. Finish each one in your own words.

When you finish, read it back and check the two golden rules: is it honest, and is it balanced (both the good and the hard)?
steps: The issue we worked on was ...
This issue is important because ...
Our goal was ...
The action we took was ...
My contribution was ...
I could have improved my contribution by ...
Working as a team helped us to ...
Working as a team was challenging because ...
One way my ideas or skills changed is ...

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your full reflection to your AI tutor.
Ask it: Is my reflection complete, honest and balanced? Which part is strongest, and which is weakest?
Ask the tutor to help you improve the weakest part until you are proud of the whole reflection.

boxes.title: Share it at home
lines: Read your finished reflection to someone at home.
Ask them what they think you have learned this year, and add anything new to your journal.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does the word 'reflection' mean?
practice.answer: Reflection means thinking in depth about an experience: what you learned, how your ideas and behaviour changed, and how you worked in your team. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: Reflection points inwards, at yourself and your ______, rather than outwards at the world.
practice.answer: Team (yourself and your teamwork).

practice.prompt: Name the four team roles.
practice.answer: Facilitator, recorder, reporter, timekeeper.

practice.prompt: Which role makes sure everyone takes part?
practice.answer: The facilitator.

practice.prompt: Which role watches the clock so the team finishes in time?
practice.answer: The timekeeper.

practice.prompt: True or false: a good reflection only talks about the parts that went well.
practice.answer: False. A good reflection is balanced: it includes what was good and what was hard.

practice.prompt: Finish the frame that shows a changed idea: 'I used to think ... but now ______'.
practice.answer: '... now I think ...' (a changed idea).

practice.prompt: When two team members do different jobs at the same time, we say they are working in ______.
practice.answer: Parallel.

practice.prompt: A complete personal reflection names the issue, the goal, the action, your ______, how to improve, and what was good and hard.
practice.answer: Contribution.

practice.prompt: Which skill does this reflection show: 'I checked whether the source could be trusted'?
practice.answer: Evaluation.

practice.prompt: Give one benefit and one challenge of working in a team.
practice.answer: Any sensible pair, such as: benefit — more ideas and shared work; challenge — people may disagree or not do their share.

practice.prompt: Constructive feedback names one thing done well and one thing to ______.
practice.answer: Improve (a clear idea for improving).

practice.prompt: Match the challenge to a solution: 'We were not sure our plan had worked.' What should the team decide before they start?
practice.answer: They should decide how they will measure success before they start.

practice.prompt: Name one thing you would write in a reflection journal.
practice.answer: Any one of: the date and project, your role, one thing that went well, one thing that was hard, or a way you improved.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why it is useful to reflect after a team project.
practice.answer: Any one of: to learn from what happened, to do better next time, or to become a stronger teammate.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each reflection word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Contribution
options: A. The team member who makes sure everyone takes part.
B. The thing you personally do to help your team.
C. Comments that are kind and helpful, naming a strength and an improvement.
D. The team member who watches the clock.
E. Doing different tasks at the same time to save time.
F. A reflection that includes both what was good and what was hard.
practice.answer: B — The thing you personally do to help your team.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Facilitator
practice.answer: A — The team member who makes sure everyone takes part.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Parallel
practice.answer: E — Doing different tasks at the same time to save time.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Constructive feedback
practice.answer: C — Comments that are kind and helpful, naming a strength and an improvement.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Balanced reflection
practice.answer: F — A reflection that includes both what was good and what was hard.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Timekeeper
practice.answer: D — The team member who watches the clock.

practice.intro: A great way to prove you understand reflection is to improve one that is not quite right. Each reflection below has a problem. Name the problem, then rewrite it so it is honest, balanced and complete.
practice.prompt: 'Our team made a poster. It was really good and I did most of the work.'
practice.answer: It sounds boastful and unfair, and it hides any hard part. A better version shares the credit and adds a challenge: 'We each took a task; I designed the poster while Nadia wrote the slogan. It was hard when we ran low on time, so next time we would start earlier.'
practice.note: Your wording will differ. Check that you spotted the problem and that your rewrite fixes it.

practice.prompt: 'Everything went wrong. My team was no help at all and I did not enjoy it.'
practice.answer: It is not balanced, because it only lists problems. A better version keeps one honest difficulty but adds a good part and a solution: 'Some jobs were left undone, which was frustrating, but we did finish the poster, and next time a clear task plan would help.'

practice.prompt: 'We did a project about bees. It was fine.'
practice.answer: It has no detail, no contribution and no learning. A better version adds them: 'I gathered three facts about why bees matter, and learned that they pollinate crops, which changed how I think about food. The hard part was keeping our facts short.'

reflection.prompt: Leila's team finished a poster, but she wrote only: 'It was good.' What two parts is her reflection missing?
reflection.modelAnswer: Her reflection is missing her own contribution and something that was hard (it also has no goal or way to improve). It is not balanced.

reflection.prompt: Sami did all the printing while, at the same time, Nadia wrote the slogan. What is this way of working called?
reflection.modelAnswer: Working in parallel (doing different tasks at the same time).

reflection.prompt: A teammate writes a reflection that only lists problems and nothing good. Is it balanced, and what would you add?
reflection.modelAnswer: No, it is not balanced. You would add at least one thing that went well, so the reflection tells the whole story.

reflection.prompt: Aran wants to give feedback on a weak reflection. Write one 'Well done for ...' and one 'Next time you could try ...' he might use.
reflection.modelAnswer: For example: 'Well done for finishing your part on time.' 'Next time you could try adding one thing that was hard.'

reflection.prompt: Aran's team was not sure their plastic-free week had worked. What should they have decided before they began?
reflection.modelAnswer: They should have decided how to measure success before they began, such as counting the rubbish before and after.

reflection.prompt: Nadia says: 'I used to think one person cannot make a difference, but now I think a team can change a lot.' Which reflection skill is she showing?
reflection.modelAnswer: She is showing Reflection: she is noticing how her ideas have changed ('I used to think ... but now I think ...').

reflection.prompt: Omar was the timekeeper but never told his team how much time was left. What could he do better next time?
reflection.modelAnswer: He could tell the team the time left at clear points, such as a warning when five minutes remain, so they finish their work.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Reflecting with my AI tutor, my reflection partner ...
Doing the real teamwork with my group in teacher sessions ...
Talking to a family member or neighbour ...
Writing in my reflection journal as I went ...

vocabulary.meaning: The way a person acts. A good reflection can show how your behaviour has changed after learning something new.
The good things you gain from doing something, such as the benefits of sharing the work in a team.
The reason something happens. Analysis and reflection often look for the cause of a problem.
The hard parts of a task, such as the challenges you meet when working as part of a team.
In a kind and helpful way. Good feedback is given constructively, naming a strength and an improvement.
The thing you personally do to help your team reach its goal.
Pieces of information that can be checked and shown to be true, unlike an opinion.
The difference something makes, such as the impact of a plastic-free week on the amount of rubbish.
Got better at something. You have improved a skill when you can do it better than before.
Thinking about something carefully and fully, not just quickly. Real reflection is done in depth.
Chances to do something useful, such as the opportunities a team project gives you to improve a skill.
To help people change their minds and choose to act, for example to use less plastic.
Things you can do well, which you build up with practice over time.
The places your information comes from, such as a book, a website or a person you ask.
The smaller jobs that together make up a whole project.
Working together with other people towards a shared goal.

mistakes: Only saying 'it was good' or 'it was fun' with no detail.
Talking only about what went well, and leaving out what was hard.
Talking only about problems, and leaving out what went well.
Forgetting to name your own contribution to the team.
Naming a challenge but never saying how you would solve it.
Giving feedback that is harsh, or feedback that is empty and says nothing useful.
